documentation.range:
This species occurs in India from west to the east south of river Ganga and north of river Godavari (in Rajasthan, Gujarat, Maharashtra, Madhya Pradesh, Telangana, Andhra Pradesh, Uttar Pradesh, Bihar, Chattisgarh, Jharkhand, Odisha, and West Bengal). The Bangladesh population is very likely to have originated from a single pair introduced by Hindu pilgrims on the bank of the River Jalangi (Delhi Gazette 2 March 1867; Molur et al. 2003; Brandon Jones 2004).

The range extends 1,900 km west to east and all population with the northern type tail carriage included.
documentation.population: The total population of this species is unknown. Most of the populations occupy human dominated landscapes, with very few actually occurring in forested areas. Negative interactions with humans are a major cause of concern and suspected declines are based on this.
documentation.habitats:
This species is mainly terrestrial, folivorous, and diurnal. It is found in a wide variety of habitats, including close to human habitations at elevations up to 400 m (Molur et al. 2003).

Dry tropical deciduous forest, tropical thorn forest in Gujarat and Rajasthan, tropical moist deciduous forest, sparsely wooded areas, scrublands, areas proximal to human habitation. 

Densities vary across the population. In Orcha, Madhya Pradesh the density was as low as 5 ind/km2 while in Kanga Tiger Reserve north of Orcha it was 45 ind/km2 and in Gir it was 121 ind/km2.
documentation.threats:
Molur et al. (2003) lists the following threats for this species: intensive agriculture, habitat loss, man animal conflict, and fires. Hunting for food by newly settled human populations in Andhra Pradesh and Odisha is very rampant and many populations are affected locally.

Sharma et al. (2010) discuss S. entellus-human interactions in Jodhpur, Rajasthan, India. The study reports of the largely misinformed attitude and behaviour of tourists towards langurs. The langurs were reported to steal food from tourists which later, as argued, could evolve to a serious threat.  In Jodhpur, langur troops with the most provisioning were found to engage in more aggressive interaction with humans than the troop with the least provisioning (Lal & Rajpurohit, 2010).In Chitrakoot, Madhya Pradesh, where langurs are provisioned as part of a religious sensibility, langurs are reported to engage in stealing food from devotees, entering dwellings and damaging property, and even crop raiding (Chaturvedi & Mishra 2014).

Crop raiding (Khatun et al. 2013), habitat change, translocation to avert crop raiding or other trouble are some of the other threats to the species in Karnataka. Kumara et al. (2010) surveyed the langur population in Dharwar-Haliyal Road in 2003, after nearly forty years of the last survey in 1961 by Sugiyama (1964) and found the number to be 38% of the last count. Hunting and trapping for consumption, monoculture plantations, tree felling are some of the reasons considered that might have affected the langur population along the years.
documentation.measures:
This species is listed on CITES Appendix I, and is on Schedule II, Part I, Indian Wildlife Protection Act, 1972 amended up to 2002, and Bangladesh: Schedule III, Bangladesh Wildlife (Preservation) (Amendment) Act, 1974 (Molur et al. 2003).

Molur et al. (2003) recommended research on taxonomy, human animal conflicts, and more surveys, as well as habitat management, wild population management, public education, monitoring, and limiting factor management.
documentation.use_trade: Hunted for food in some areas of its range.
documentation.rationale: Listed as Least Concern in view of its wide distribution, tolerance of a broad range of habitats, presumed large population, and because it is unlikely to be declining fast enough to qualify for listing in a more threatened category. If threats arising from hunting and human-animal interactions increase, this species will need to be reassessed, and could qualify for listing as Near Threatened.
documentation.taxonomic_notes: Monotypic. Show wide variation in coat colouration across their distribution but little genetic variation. Semnopithecus entellus sport the ‘Northern Type’ tail carriage, looped in the front. The tail either touches the back or falls on either side of the body.
